title: The Resurrection Predictions

keyTerms.d: “Prophecy from the outcome”: on this critical reading, the “predictions” are not Jesus reading the future but the evangelists reading the past — composing or, more plausibly, sharpening sayings so that Jesus’ death and resurrection appear foreordained. For the detailed predictions, this is not a fringe view; it is a widely held critical position — though it works least well against the rough edges.

Material the early church would have found awkward, and so had no motive to invent, has a stronger claim to be historical. Around the passion predictions, the tradition preserves the disciples’ dullness and desertion — an unflattering portrait of the very men who became the church’s pillars.

The temple saying appears independently in Mark and John, two streams many scholars treat as largely separate. More telling, it surfaces not as a triumphant Christian slogan but as an accusation used against Jesus at his trial and as a taunt at his execution.

Pressed for a miraculous proof, Jesus refuses and offers only a cipher. It is a riddle the Gospel writers themselves had to interpret — and interpreted differently. That very untidiness is a mark of antiquity: the saying looks like something handed down and puzzled over, not engineered.
Jesus’ exact words. We cannot reconstruct them, and we should not pretend to. The label “contested” belongs on any claim that Jesus foretold the resurrection in specific terms.

Jewish idiom counted part of a day as the whole (compare Esther 4:16 with 5:1): Friday, Saturday and Sunday could make “three days,” and “after three days” / “on the third day” could name one interval.

The ex eventu explanation works best against the clear, detailed predictions — and least well against the awkward features. A theory that explains the polished predictions by invention must still explain why the rough edges survived — and invention is a poor explanation of rough edges.

Not a standalone proof. It coheres with the larger case for the resurrection — the empty tomb, the appearances, the transformation of the disciples — and lends it texture; it does not bear the weight alone.

derive.q: After each prediction in Mark, the disciples conspicuously fail — Peter rebukes Jesus, the Twelve argue about who is greatest, two angle for thrones, and at the end all flee — so the frame is…?
derive.ans: embarrassing — the wrong move for an inventor
derive.why: If a later community were fabricating prophecies to glorify its founder, the natural move would be to show the disciples grasping and trusting them. Instead the tradition preserves their dullness and desertion — an unflattering portrait of the very men who became the church’s pillars.

derive.q: The temple saying turns up as the charge at his trial and a taunt at the cross — so it reads as…?
derive.ans: awkward, hostile attestation — not a Christian slogan
derive.why: A community inventing a prediction to prove its founder divine would not naturally cast it as the charge that helped get him killed. The embarrassment runs the right direction for authenticity.

derive.q: “The sign of Jonah” is a riddle that Matthew ties to three days in the earth and Luke leaves as Jonah-the-preacher to Nineveh — so the saying is…?
derive.ans: handed down and puzzled over, not engineered
derive.why: If you were manufacturing a proof-text after Easter, you would write a clear one. “On the third day I will rise” is clear. “The sign of Jonah” is a riddle that the Gospel writers themselves had to interpret — and interpreted differently. That very untidiness is a mark of antiquity.

derive.q: The third prediction reads like a checklist of the passion narrative that follows it — condemnation, Gentiles, mockery, spitting, flogging — so the detailed predictions are…?
derive.ans: plausibly sharpened in the telling — concede it
derive.why: The honest apologist should concede what is accurate here. The detailed third prediction may well have been sharpened. The neat “after three days” formula likely owes some of its precision to hindsight and to Hosea 6:2. We cannot reconstruct Jesus’ exact words, and we should not pretend to.

derive.q: Invention explains the polished predictions. Does it explain why the riddle, the disciples’ failure and the hostile temple charge survived?
derive.ans: no — invention is a poor explanation of rough edges
derive.why: If the evangelists were freely composing prophecies to fit the outcome, why leave the sign of Jonah a riddle? Why preserve the disciples’ failure to understand? Why let the temple saying stand as a hostile accusation rather than a Christian creed? A theory that explains the polished predictions by invention must still explain why the rough edges survived.

derive.q: The Gospels came decades later — but the creed Paul hands on was being confessed within a few years of the crucifixion. So the creed shows…?
derive.ans: the vindication was proclaimed from the start (not that the predictions were spoken before Easter)
derive.why: The creed of 1 Corinthians 15:3–7 shows that within a few years of the crucifixion the earliest Christians were already confessing his death, burial, resurrection, and appearances. It forecloses the easy theory that the resurrection was a legend grown ripe over generations. That does not show the predictions were spoken before Easter; it shows the vindication they point to was proclaimed from the start.

honestState.p1: The field has moved, but not to a consensus. A generation ago, under Bultmann’s shadow, the passion predictions were near-automatically dismissed. In recent decades scholars have grown more willing to grant that Jesus foresaw his death, and many are at least open to some authentic core behind the resurrection predictions. Sanders’ verdict on the temple saying is widely shared. But the detailed predictions remain, for most critical scholars, partly shaped after the fact.
honestState.fairness: A robust skeptical wing, with Ehrman among its best-known spokesmen, holds the whole package loosely. There is no scholarly consensus that Jesus predicted his resurrection in specific terms, and an honest reader should not be told there is. The skeptic who says the detailed predictions may have been sharpened in the telling raises a possibility the evidence cannot rule out, and the believer who insists the Gospels preserve his predictions verbatim overreaches.
honestState.verdict: Our answer to the question is yes, in the form the evidence reaches: Jesus went to Jerusalem expecting to die and foretold, in veiled terms, that God would vindicate him beyond death. That expectation was not a disappointed hope. This is a supporting strand, not a standalone proof: the resurrection itself rests on other grounds — the early creed of 1 Corinthians 15:3–7, the empty tomb, the appearances — and on those grounds we hold that God raised him bodily.

order: Before the end Jesus spoke of a coming death and a vindication beyond it.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its precision limit.
cards.a: Before the end Jesus spoke of a coming death and a vindication beyond it — in the passion predictions, the riddling sign of Jonah, and the temple saying. The argument is not that these texts are clear prophecies of Easter; the label “contested” belongs on any claim that he foretold the resurrection in specific terms.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and what kind of result it supports.
cards.a: The predictions are authenticated by embarrassment: material the early church would have found awkward, and so had no motive to invent, has a stronger claim to be historical. It supports a defensible historical core — not proof of detailed foreknowledge.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That Jesus went to Jerusalem expecting to die and foretold, in veiled terms, that God would vindicate him. It does not, on its own, prove detailed foreknowledge of the resurrection: this is a supporting strand, not a standalone proof.

cards.q: Why does the disciples’ behaviour around the predictions count as evidence?
cards.a: After each prediction they conspicuously fail — rebuking him, arguing about greatness, angling for thrones — and at the end they flee. A community fabricating prophecies to glorify its founder would show the disciples grasping and trusting them; instead the tradition preserves their dullness and desertion.

cards.q: Why is the temple saying’s setting evidence for authenticity?
cards.a: It appears independently in two streams many scholars treat as largely separate, and it surfaces as an accusation at the trial and a taunt at the execution. A community inventing a prediction to prove its founder divine would not cast it as the charge that helped get him killed.

cards.q: Why does the untidiness of the Jonah saying count for it?
cards.a: A manufactured proof-text would be clear. This is a riddle the Gospel writers themselves had to interpret, and interpreted differently. It looks like something handed down and puzzled over, not engineered.

cards.q: State the “prophecy after the event” objection at full strength.
cards.a: The Gospels were written decades after the events, by believers who already knew how the story ended; on this reading the predictions are the evangelists reading the past, composing or sharpening sayings so the outcome looks foreordained. The third prediction reads like a checklist of the passion narrative. For the detailed predictions this is a widely held critical position, and the independent, pre-Easter witness is exactly what we do not have.

cards.q: What should the honest apologist concede to that objection?
cards.a: The detailed third prediction may well have been sharpened; the neat “after three days” formula likely owes some of its precision to hindsight and to a prophetic text about rising on the third day; and we cannot reconstruct his exact words and should not pretend to.

cards.q: Where is the deflationary case’s soft seam?
cards.a: It works best against the clear, detailed predictions and least well against the awkward features — the riddle left a riddle, the disciples’ failure preserved, the temple saying left as a hostile charge. A theory that explains the polish by invention must still explain why the rough edges survived.

cards.q: Why is a Jesus who expected suffering and vindication not a Christian back-projection?
cards.a: Because even on a skeptical apocalyptic reading his message announced coming judgment and the vindication of the righteous. On our reading, then, such a Jesus is a thoroughly Jewish, thoroughly first-century figure: one need not believe in fulfilled prophecy to believe a condemned prophet anticipated his fate.

cards.q: What does the early creed add to this argument — and what does it not add?
cards.a: It shows that within a few years of the crucifixion the earliest Christians were already confessing his death, burial, resurrection, and appearances — foreclosing the legend-over-generations theory. It does not show the predictions were spoken before Easter; it shows the vindication they point to was proclaimed from the start.

The field has moved, but not to a consensus: scholars are more willing to grant that Jesus foresaw his death, and many are open to an authentic core, but the detailed predictions remain, for most critical scholars, partly shaped after the fact. There is no consensus that he predicted his resurrection in specific terms, and an honest reader should not be told there is.

obj.q: Convenient that the predictions were written down after the alleged fulfilment. The Gospels came decades later, from believers who knew the ending — the third prediction is just the passion narrative run backwards: condemnation, Gentiles, mockery, spitting, flogging.
obj.model: Concede what is accurate: the detailed third prediction may well have been sharpened, the neat “after three days” formula likely owes some of its precision to hindsight and to Hosea 6:2, and we cannot reconstruct Jesus’ exact words. But the deflationary case has a soft seam. It works best against the clear, detailed predictions — and least well against the awkward features. If the evangelists were freely composing prophecies to fit the outcome, why leave the sign of Jonah a riddle? Why preserve the disciples’ failure to understand? Why let the temple saying stand as a hostile accusation rather than a Christian creed? Invention is a poor explanation of rough edges. And the “decades later” frame leaves out our earliest evidence: the creed of 1 Corinthians 15:3–7 shows the vindication was proclaimed from the start — though that does not show the predictions were spoken before Easter. The critic keeps a real foothold: the gap between “Jesus anticipated vindication in veiled terms” and “Jesus prophesied his bodily resurrection on the third day” is wide. But what survives is real, early, and not the after-the-fact invention the deflationary reading needs.

obj.q: Mark says “after three days,” Matthew says “on the third day,” and Matthew 12:40 says “three days and three nights” — yet he died Friday and rose Sunday, barely a day and a half. The math fails the prophecy.
obj.model: Jewish idiom counted part of a day as the whole (compare Esther 4:16 with 5:1): Friday, Saturday and Sunday could make “three days,” and “after three days” / “on the third day” could name one interval. Matthew keeps both phrases pages apart without anxiety. And the “three days and three nights” wrinkle is at least as consistent with an inherited saying the writers felt bound to preserve as with free invention, since a fabricator working only from hindsight had no need to leave the wrinkle in.

obj.q: If he predicted it publicly, the disciples were primed — they hallucinated what they expected, or staged the fulfilment. Your prediction premise feeds the naturalistic theories.
obj.model: The texts you need for the predictions also record the expectation failing to form — incomprehension, flight, spices for a corpse, scepticism at the first reports. Priming that produced no expectation is a poor seedbed for hallucinations of exactly that. As for staging: a hoax is a poor fit for men who went on proclaiming it, under threat, in the city of the execution. The disciples’ failure to understand also answers the sharpest rejoinder — if Jesus foretold his rising, why did no one wait at the tomb? — because the tradition itself says they did not understand him (Mark 9:32), an embarrassing admission about the church’s own pillars rather than a flattering invention.

obj.q: He also said “this generation will not pass away” before the Son of Man comes — a famous miss. A prophet with a failed prediction gets no credit for an alleged hit.
obj.model: On a widely held reading, “this generation” governs what the discourse itself calls “these things” — the Temple’s destruction, “not one stone on another” — which happened in AD 70, inside the generation; Christians differ on how much else the discourse covers, and we do not adjudicate between them. On that reading, the discourse separates “these things” from “that day or that hour,” of which “no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (Mark 13:32) — the Son’s not knowing the hour belongs to the genuine limits of his human consciousness, not to a deficiency in the divine nature he never ceased to possess. On that reading it is a hit rather than a miss. And methodologically: the death-and-vindication sayings stand or fall on their own evidence.

unseen.q: Why all the hedging? Mark 10 lists the mockery, the spitting, the flogging — and it all came true. That proves he knew the future, which proves he is God. Lead with the detailed prediction.
unseen.model: Lead with it and you lead with the weakest card. The clearest predictions are the ones most vulnerable to the charge of hindsight, and the survivors of the critical filter are precisely the vaguest — the detailed third prediction may well have been sharpened in the telling. So this argument does not, on its own, prove that Jesus possessed detailed foreknowledge of the resurrection, still less that such foreknowledge demonstrates his divinity; that is a limit on this argument, not on who he is. The believer who insists the Gospels preserve his predictions verbatim overreaches. Lead instead with what survives the sharpest criticism: a Jesus who went up to Jerusalem expecting to die and to be vindicated by God — real, early, and not the after-the-fact invention the deflationary reading needs. It is a supporting strand that coheres with the larger case; the resurrection itself rests on the early creed of 1 Corinthians 15:3–7, the empty tomb and the appearances, and on those grounds we hold that God raised him bodily.
